processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under argon were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm; plates then cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 samples by electrical discharge machining.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon, followed by oil quenching; parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq.

The solution-treated 15Al samples were aged at temperatures between 525 °C and 650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h, followed by water quenching; this sample is the 575 °C / 10 h condition. Table 2 lists the 575 °C aging series of the 15Al alloy with columns 1 h, 3 h, 6 h, 10 h.

characterization_methods.key_findings: The 15Al alloy aged at 575 °C for 10 h shows 957.8 ± 10.1 HV (Table 2), part of the 253.4–965.6 HV ultra-wide hardness window; aging at 575 °C and above accelerates the hardening response substantially.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load 9.8 N for 15 s; 5 repeated measurements per sample averaged; samples electrolytically polished (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol)
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the Vickers hardness of the 15Al alloy after each aging treatment and construct the aging-hardening (hardness vs time/temperature) data set.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 15Al 575 °C–10 h condition the matrix is an essentially uniform, featureless β-Mn material in which only a 10 μm inset reveals fine 'new precipitates'; the α → β-Mn transformation of 15Al proceeds fastest at higher aging temperatures.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: electrolytically polished samples; main fields with 50 μm scale bars, higher-magnification insets with 10 μm scale bars (Fig. 7)
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the precipitation of secondary phases (α-Mn and β-Mn) and follow the α → β-Mn transformation in the 15Al alloy with aging time and temperature.

phases_present.morphology: essentially uniform matrix; the short rod-shaped β-Mn that nucleated along α grain boundaries and inside α grains grew until precipitates came into contact with each other, giving a featureless field at 50 μm
fine new precipitates within the β-Mn matrix
fine particles distributed at the interfaces between β-Mn (with FCC twins)

precipitates.distribution: within the transformed β-Mn matrix and at the β-Mn interfaces; visible only in the 10 μm inset of the 575 °C–10 h SE-SEM field
precipitates.type: fine 'new precipitates' (BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases)

structures.overall_structure: After aging at 575 °C for 10 h the α matrix of the 15Al alloy is almost completely transformed into β-Mn; the SE-SEM field of this condition is an essentially uniform, featureless β-Mn matrix at the 50 μm scale, containing fine so-called 'new precipitates' resolvable only in a 10 μm inset. EBSD/TEM (performed on other conditions of the same alloy) show such ultra-hard states consist of β-Mn plus new BCC and FCC (Cu-rich) phases at the β-Mn interfaces.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester at a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and the hardness given as the average of 5 measurements.
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 sample (electrolytically polished with 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol)

unmapped_findings: The 575 °C/10 h condition of the 15Al alloy was not the state used for the detailed TEM/EBSD characterization: TEM was performed on 15Al aged at 600 °C for 6 h (965.6 HV) and 17Al aged at 575 °C for 6 h (924.9 HV), and the EBSD maps of 15Al in Fig. 4 correspond to 525 °C/3 h, 550 °C/6 h and 650 °C/3 h. Microstructural information specific to the 575 °C/10 h sample therefore comes only from the SE-SEM panel (Fig. 7) and the general aging sequence description.

Within the 15Al aging series at 575 °C (same temperature, sibling samples not this one), hardness was 752.6 ± 50.7 HV at 1 h, 935.5 ± 15.8 HV at 3 h, 960.3 ± 6.8 HV at 6 h and 957.8 ± 10.1 HV at 10 h; i.e. the 575 °C series peaks at 6 h, and the 10 h sample studied here is just below that peak.

For the ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloys the volume fraction of the FCC Cu-rich + BCC precipitates at the β-Mn interfaces increases with Al content: 3.9 % for 15Al aged at 650 °C for 3 h (852.3 HV), 4.7 % for 17Al aged at 650 °C for 10 h (833.2 HV) and 6.5 % for 19Al aged at 650 °C for 6 h (810.9 HV). These values are for sibling 650 °C conditions, not the 575 °C/10 h sample.

The microstructural evolution sequence reported for the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels during aging is α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase; at 575 °C a significant amount of β-Mn formed after just 1 h of aging, and at 600 °C and above the α matrix almost completely transformed into β-Mn within 1 h.

The density of the 15Al alloy (alloy-level, not aged-sample-level) was measured by the Archimedes method as 6.85 g·cm−3; the highest specific hardness of 141 HV·cm3/g was reported for the peak-hardness Fe-35.2Mn-15Al-5.2Cu state (965.6 HV at 600 °C/6 h), not for the 575 °C/10 h sample.
